python.def: The programming language the course uses. It reads a text file of instructions and runs them one line at a time.
levels: Python is a language for talking to the computer, like a very picky friend who only understands exact words and gets confused by typos. You write a list of instructions in a file, and the computer follows them in order, one at a time, like a recipe. If you tell it to mix the eggs before cracking them, it will try anyway and something will go wrong.

Python is a programming language: a set of words and punctuation rules for writing instructions that a computer can run. You save the instructions in a file ending in `.py`, and running `python script.py` makes the computer read that file top to bottom and do what it says. It is popular because the rules are close to plain English, and there are ready-made toolkits (libraries) for almost anything, including reading traffic data and building models.

Python is an interpreted language: `python script.py` reads the file and executes it line by line, rather than compiling it into a separate program first. Variables are created by assignment (`x = 5`), functions by `def`, and indentation, not braces, marks which lines belong to a loop, function, or if-statement. A single misplaced indent changes what the code means, which is unusual compared to languages like C or Java. Errors show as a traceback: the last few lines usually name the file, the line number, and what went wrong.

Python is dynamically typed, meaning a variable's type is checked at run time, not in advance, and garbage-collected, which trades some raw speed for fast, readable code, a fair trade for data science, where the real cost is usually reading files and calling into fast libraries such as numpy and pandas that are themselves written in C. The reference implementation, CPython, has a Global Interpreter Lock that prevents true multi-threaded parallelism for Python code, though numeric libraries route around it by releasing the lock during their own C code. Its ecosystem, pandas for tables, scikit-learn for classical models, PyTorch for neural networks, is why it dominates ML, not raw language speed. It fails or frustrates when a task needs real parallel CPU work in pure Python, or when a project's dependency versions drift and code that worked last year no longer runs.

The GIL forces a choice: use multiple processes instead of threads for CPU-bound parallelism, or lean on libraries that release it, which is why `multiprocessing`, joblib, and vectorized numpy or pandas calls matter more than Python's own loops for performance. Type hints (`def f(x: int) -> float`) do not change what runs; they only let tools like mypy catch mistakes before execution, so they are documentation with teeth, not real static typing. A common mistake is writing row-by-row Python loops over a pandas DataFrame instead of vectorized operations, which can be a hundred times slower for the same result. Packaging and environments, the actual versions of Python and its libraries, matter as much as the code itself, because the same script can give different numeric results on different machines.

At production scale, Python is usually the orchestration and modeling layer, while the inner loops that matter for speed are compiled: numpy and PyTorch call into C, C++, and CUDA or Metal kernels. Projects like Cython, Numba, and a no-GIL build of CPython (PEP 703) are ongoing attempts to close the gap without leaving the language. The open question in industry is less whether Python is fast enough and more whether a huge, dynamically typed codebase can stay correct as it grows, which is why large Python codebases invest heavily in type checking and testing infrastructure the language itself does not require.

git.def: The version-control tool. It records snapshots (commits) of your files so you can see history, undo, and branch. GitHub hosts repositories online.
levels: Git is a magic notebook for your project that remembers every version of your work. Every time you save a snapshot, called a commit, the notebook writes down what changed and lets you flip back to any earlier page. GitHub is like a shelf in the cloud where you can keep a copy of the notebook so it does not get lost.

Git is a tool that tracks changes to your files over time. You take a snapshot with `git commit -m "message"`, and `git log` shows every snapshot you have ever taken, in order. If you break something, you can look back through the history and see exactly what changed and when. GitHub is a website that stores a copy of your Git history online, so you can share it or work on it from another computer.

Git has three areas: the working tree, your files as you see them, the staging area, what `git add` has queued for the next snapshot, and the repository, the committed history. `git status` shows which files are staged, unstaged, or untracked; `git diff` shows exact line changes before you commit. Branches are just movable pointers to a commit, so `git branch` and `git checkout -b` let you try something without touching the main line of work. A `.gitignore` file lists patterns, like `data/` or `.env`, that Git should never track, which keeps large data files and secrets out of history.

Git commits form a directed acyclic graph, each commit pointing to its parent, or parents, for a merge, which is what makes history browsable and branches mergeable. A branch name is only a label on a commit; merging combines two histories, and rebasing rewrites one branch's commits to sit on top of another instead. Git tracks content, not files by name, so renaming a file is detected by comparing content, not recorded as a special operation. Workflow habits, small commits, clear messages, reviewing your own diff before committing, matter more for solo reproducibility than any single Git feature, because the log is only useful if it is honest about what changed and why.

Internally, Git stores every version as a content-addressed object, blobs for file contents, trees for directory structure, commits for snapshots, each named by the hash of its content, so two identical files anywhere in history are stored once. The reflog records where branch tips have pointed, even after a rebase, reset, or deleted branch, which makes almost anything recoverable for a while even when the visible history looks gone. `git bisect` does binary search over commits to find which one introduced a bug or, in ML work, changed a metric, far faster than checking commits one by one. A common mistake is committing large binary data or model checkpoints directly, which bloats the repository forever, since Git's history is append-only and rewriting it after the fact is disruptive.

At scale, plain Git strains under huge monorepos and large binary artifacts, which is why organizations add Git LFS, partial clones, or move data and model files to separate versioning systems that store lineage without bloating the Git object store. Code review at scale is built on top of Git, not inside it; pull requests, required checks, and blame tooling all sit outside Git's own model of commits and branches. An open practical problem is tying together the two histories that matter for a reproducible ML result, the code history in Git and the data and model history in whatever system tracks those, so that a commit hash alone is not enough to reproduce a claim.

launchd.def: macOS's built-in scheduler. A plist in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` tells it to run a program every N seconds or at boot, with logs to named files.
levels: launchd is like an alarm clock built into a Mac that can wake up a program instead of a person. You tell it when to run something, every so often, or the moment the computer turns on, and it remembers, even while you are asleep.

launchd is the part of macOS that starts programs on a schedule or at login, instead of you having to remember to run them yourself. You describe the job in a small settings file called a plist, saved in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, which says what program to run and how often. Loading it with `launchctl load` tells macOS to start watching the clock; from then on the job runs automatically, even if you never open a terminal.

A launchd plist is an XML file with keys like `ProgramArguments`, the command to run, `StartInterval`, seconds between runs, and `StandardOutPath`/`StandardErrorPath`, where logs go. You load it with `launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.you.job.plist` and check it is running with `launchctl list | grep job`. Unlike cron, launchd can also run a job at login, at wake, or whenever a file changes, not just on a fixed clock.

launchd is macOS's single service manager for both user jobs, LaunchAgents, running as you, with access to your desktop session, and system jobs, LaunchDaemons, running as root, without a session, which replaced the older cron and init on macOS. Because agents run only while a user is logged in, a job that must run overnight on a laptop also needs `caffeinate` to stop the machine sleeping, or it silently never fires. Errors typically show up not as a crash but as a missing log file, an empty output file, or a job listed with a nonzero last exit code in `launchctl list`. It fails quietly when the plist has a syntax error, a wrong path, or when macOS's permission system blocks the job from reading files it needs.

A recurring silent failure on macOS is Full Disk Access: a launchd job runs, but the script it calls cannot read files in protected locations unless the terminal or Python binary that launchd invokes has been explicitly granted access in System Settings, and the job fails with a permissions error deep in its own log rather than a launchd error. `StartInterval` fires roughly every N seconds from load time, not on the wall-clock schedule a `StartCalendarInterval` gives you, so the two are easy to confuse when precise timing matters. Because agents only run in a login session, unattended data-collection jobs on a personal Mac are more fragile than the same job on a server, and practitioners often discover this only when a week of expected data is missing. A `KeepAlive` key can restart a crashing job forever, which turns a silent bug into a fast, repeated failure that fills logs rather than showing an obvious crash.

In production, cron-like scheduling on a single machine does not scale to the retraining and monitoring jobs a real pipeline needs; the equivalent problems are solved by workflow schedulers with retries, alerting, and dependency graphs between jobs, none of which launchd provides. launchd remains useful for exactly the case this course uses it for, a personal machine collecting data unattended, where the tradeoffs of sleep, permissions, and no dependency graph are acceptable. The open, unglamorous problem in real deployments is the same one at any scale: knowing when a scheduled job silently stopped working, not just when it crashed loudly.

postmile.def: A station's distance along its freeway, used to put stations in driving order and find neighbors.
levels: Every station on the freeway has a number that says how far along the road it is, like mile markers on a long hiking trail. If you line the stations up by that number, you know which one comes right before or after another as you drive.

Postmile is the distance, in miles, from the start of a freeway to a given detector station. PeMS stores this as a column called `Abs_PM` in its station metadata. Because postmile increases along the direction of travel, sorting stations by postmile within the same freeway and direction puts them in the order a car would actually pass them, which is how you figure out which station is upstream or downstream of another.

To build a station's neighbors, you filter the station table to the same freeway and direction, sort by `Abs_PM`, and take the row immediately before, upstream, and after, downstream, in that sorted order. Two stations can share a freeway number but be on opposite directions, `N` versus `S`, so direction has to match before postmile comparisons mean anything. A gap in postmile between neighbors, say five miles instead of half a mile, is a sign that a station is missing or was decommissioned, not that the freeway physically jumped.

Postmile is a 1-D coordinate along a specific freeway-and-direction, computed from Caltrans's official mile markers, and it is what makes upstream and downstream well-defined without needing real latitude and longitude geometry. Building the neighbor graph reduces to a groupby-sort-shift: group by freeway and direction, sort by postmile, and the row above and below each station in that ordering are its neighbors. It fails at freeway interchanges, where a driver can physically move between two different postmile sequences, transitioning from one freeway to another, so a purely postmile-based neighbor graph misses those connections. It also assumes postmile is monotonic along physical distance, which mostly holds but has known discontinuities where Caltrans re-surveyed a route.

Postmile order is a reasonable proxy for the next station a car reaches, but it silently drops the graph structure at freeway junctions, on-ramps, and off-ramps, which is exactly where traffic often actually originates, so lag and neighbor features built purely from postmile can miss the true causal upstream stations near an interchange. A subtler issue is that postmile resets or has small overlaps at some county or route boundaries in the raw Caltrans data, so blindly sorting the full statewide table by postmile without first grouping by freeway and direction produces nonsense neighbors. Distance in postmile also is not travel time: a mile of stop-and-go surface street feels different from a mile of open freeway, so treating postmile gaps as exchangeable across corridors is an approximation practitioners should sanity check against typical speeds on that stretch.

Real traffic systems eventually replace a 1-D postmile ordering with an actual road network graph, nodes and edges with real connectivity, including ramps and merges, because that is what graph neural network approaches to traffic forecasting need and what interchange effects require. The open modeling question this course's later graph-model lessons approach is how much predictive value that fuller graph adds over the cheap postmile-neighbor approximation, and for the Fremont corridor specifically, whether the added complexity earns its keep given how sparse true interchange effects are in the data.

grid.def: Every station × every slot, with no gaps. Missing readings are kept as NaN rows, never skipped, so shifts and windows stay aligned.
levels: Imagine an empty egg carton with a spot for every station and every five minutes of the day. Even if an egg is missing from one spot, you leave that spot empty instead of squishing the other eggs together to hide the gap, so every spot still means the same time for every station.

A grid is a table with one row for every combination of station and time slot, even when a reading is missing for that combination. Instead of skipping missing readings, the grid keeps an empty row, marked NaN, meaning not a number, in its place. This matters because later steps, like looking at the reading from 15 minutes ago, only make sense if every row really is 5 minutes apart from the next, with nothing quietly missing.

Building the grid means creating every station and timestamp pair for the full date range and 5-minute frequency, then joining the real readings onto it, so any station-slot combination without a real reading ends up as a row of NaNs rather than a missing row. In pandas this is typically a multi-index reindex over stations and timestamps. Checking `df.groupby("station_id").size()` after building the grid should show the same count for every station; if the minimum count is below the expected number of slots, some station has fewer rows than it should, meaning the grid was built wrong, not that data is missing, since missing data still gets a NaN row.

The grid exists because time-series feature engineering, `shift`, `rolling`, lag features, silently assumes every row is exactly one time step from its neighbor; if missing readings were simply dropped, a `shift(3)` would grab a reading from an arbitrary, wrong number of minutes back instead of 15 minutes back. Constructing it correctly requires a full cross product of stations and time slots rather than only the rows present in the raw file, often a large majority of the table for a corridor with many detectors over months of data. It fails when the assumed time index is wrong, for example daylight saving transitions creating a repeated or skipped hour, which breaks the every-row-a-fixed-step-apart assumption even after building a nominally complete grid. Memory is a real cost: a full grid for many stations over months at 5-minute resolution is large, and holding several copies of it during a naive groupby-shift can exhaust memory on real hardware.

The grid is really a design decision about how to represent missingness so it survives downstream computation instead of silently corrupting it, and the choice to use NaN rather than dropping rows or forward-filling matters because forward-filling before building lag features would let a stale reading masquerade as a fresh one. A related but different failure mode is when a station's sensor is broken for an extended stretch: the grid faithfully keeps those slots as NaN, and a downstream model needs an explicit strategy, drop, impute, or a missingness indicator feature, rather than pretending they do not exist. Practitioners commonly get the shape check wrong by comparing total row counts instead of per-station counts, which can hide the case where one station is missing many rows and another has duplicates that happen to cancel out in the total. The grid also implicitly assumes station identity and its associated metadata, freeway, direction, postmile, are stable over time, which breaks if a station is renumbered or moved mid-dataset.

At production scale, materializing a full dense grid for a large sensor network is often wasteful, since real-world sparsity, offline sensors, deployment gaps, can mean the true rectangle is mostly empty; production pipelines instead often keep a sparse representation and only densify a windowed slice at feature-computation time, computing lag and rolling features directly against a proper time index instead of a fully materialized table. The open engineering problem is doing this efficiently in a streaming setting, where every station and every slot needs to be maintained incrementally as new 5-minute readings arrive, rather than rebuilt from scratch, and where late-arriving or corrected readings must be reconciled without breaking already-computed downstream features.

pandas.def: The Python library for tables. `pd.read_csv`, `read_parquet`, `groupby`, `merge`, `shift`, `rolling` are its verbs.
levels: pandas is a toolkit for working with big lists that look like a spreadsheet, with rows and columns. It can read a table from a file, sort it, and let you look at just the rows you care about, much faster than doing it by hand.

pandas is a Python library, a bundle of ready-made code, for working with tables of data. You load it with `import pandas as pd`, then read a file with `pd.read_csv("file.csv")`, which gives you a DataFrame, rows and named columns, like a spreadsheet you can control with code. From there you can filter rows, add new columns, or compute summaries like an average, all with one line of code instead of writing a loop yourself.

A pandas DataFrame is a 2-D table with a row index and named columns, each column its own array of a single data type, int, float, string, datetime. Core operations include `df["speed"] > 30`, a boolean mask for filtering, `df.groupby("station_id").mean()`, aggregate per group, `df.merge(other, on="station_id")`, join two tables, and `df["speed"].shift(3)`, shift a column down by 3 rows, useful for value 15 minutes ago at 5-minute steps. `df.dtypes` shows each column's type, and mismatched types are a frequent source of bugs, such as a timestamp column that loaded as text instead of a datetime.

pandas is built on numpy, so its speed comes from vectorized operations, applying a function to a whole column at once in compiled code, rather than Python loops over rows, which are typically 10 to 100 times slower for the same computation. Its object model has real subtleties: a slice of a DataFrame can be a view or a copy of the underlying data depending on how it was produced, which is the source of the notorious SettingWithCopyWarning. Time-series operations like `shift` and `rolling` assume the rows are already sorted and evenly spaced in time; applied to unsorted or gappy data, they silently produce wrong answers rather than raising an error. It fails, or at least misleads, on large data primarily through memory: a DataFrame typically uses several times the raw file size in RAM, and naive code that keeps multiple intermediate copies during a groupby-shift can exceed available memory well before the raw data would suggest.

`groupby` followed by `shift` or `rolling` should be applied within each group, `df.groupby("station_id")["speed"].shift(3)`, not on the whole table at once, or values leak across station boundaries, a classic and easy mistake that produces a plausible-looking but wrong lag feature. pandas 2.x's optional Arrow-backed dtypes and nullable integer types change some of these performance and correctness tradeoffs, proper NA handling for integers, less memory for strings, but are not yet the default, so most code still lives with float64-only NaN semantics, where an integer column touched by any missing value silently becomes float. Method chaining versus intermediate variables is a real style tradeoff: chains are compact but harder to debug, since inserting a print or breakpoint mid-chain requires restructuring the code. A frequent practitioner mistake is comparing floats for exact equality after a groupby or merge, when floating-point aggregation can introduce tiny differences that make equality comparisons fail unpredictably.

At production data-pipeline scale, pandas's single-machine, in-memory model is the limiting factor, which is why teams move to Arrow-native tools or distributed systems once a table stops fitting comfortably in RAM or a job needs to run in parallel across machines. pandas remains dominant for the get-from-a-few-files-to-a-clean-feature-table phase of a project because of its ecosystem, nearly every ML and visualization library expects a DataFrame-shaped input, even as faster engines take over the heavy transforms underneath it. The open practical tension in real ML pipelines is keeping the same feature logic correct and identical between an interactive pandas prototype and whatever faster or distributed engine eventually replaces it in production, since subtle semantic differences, NaN handling, join behavior, sort stability, between engines are a common source of train and serve skew.

groupby.def: Split a table into groups by a key, compute something per group, and combine. `groupby("station_id").size()` counts rows per station.
levels: Imagine sorting a big pile of toys into bins by color, then counting how many are in each bin. groupby is the computer doing that sorting-and-counting for you, but with rows of a table instead of toys.

groupby splits a table into smaller groups based on a column's value, does something to each group separately, and then puts the results back together. `df.groupby("station_id").size()` splits the table into one group per station and counts how many rows are in each group. This pattern, split, apply a computation, combine the results, is called split-apply-combine, and it is one of the most common things you do with a table.

The general form is `df.groupby(key).agg(function)`, where key is one or more columns and function is something like mean, sum, size, or a custom function. `df.groupby("station_id")["speed"].mean()` gives the average speed for each station, as a new smaller table indexed by station_id. You can group by more than one column at once, like `df.groupby(["station_id", "hour"])`, to compute something per station per hour. `describe()` chained after a groupby is a fast way to check every station has roughly the same number of rows.

Internally, groupby builds an index mapping each group key to the row positions belonging to it, then applies the aggregation function to each group's slice; for a built-in aggregation like mean or sum, pandas uses a fast, vectorized path, but a custom Python function passed via `.apply()` falls back to a slow per-group Python call. Grouping keys can include multiple columns, producing a MultiIndex on the result, which then needs `reset_index()` to turn back into flat columns for merging elsewhere. A frequent correctness bug is calling `shift` or `rolling` on the whole table when the intent was per-group; the fix is `df.groupby(key)[col].shift(n)`, which resets the window at every group boundary instead of sliding across them. It fails to produce a meaningful result silently, not with an error, when a NaN key value is dropped from the groups by default, quietly discarding those rows from the output.

`.transform()` versus `.apply()` versus `.agg()` are subtly different: agg returns one row per group, transform returns a result the same length as the input aligned back to the original rows, useful for something like each row's deviation from its station's mean, and apply is the general but slowest escape hatch that can return either shape depending on what the function does. A groupby-shift on a large table can be memory-expensive because pandas may hold the grouped index, the sorted intermediate, and the output simultaneously; sorting the DataFrame by the group key first and using a lower-level approach is a common optimization once this becomes a bottleneck. `observed=True` matters for categorical group keys: by default groupby can materialize every combination of categories, including ones that never occur in the data, wasting memory and confusing downstream code that did not expect empty groups. Practitioners commonly get burned by silently changed row order: a naive groupby-then-concat can reorder rows relative to the original table, which breaks code downstream that assumed positional alignment.

At scale, groupby-shaped computations are exactly what distributed engines reimplement with partitioning strategies designed to avoid shuffling all of one group's data onto a single machine, which single-machine pandas does not need to worry about but which becomes the dominant cost once data is sharded across a cluster. Feature stores in production ML systems are largely built around precomputing groupby aggregations, per-user, per-station, per-item, because computing them on the fly at prediction latency is too slow; the open engineering problem is keeping those precomputed aggregations correctly time-bounded, so a feature used to predict at time t never accidentally includes information from after t.
An f-string is a fill-in-the-blank sentence. You write "My name is ___" and the computer drops your actual name into the blank for you, every time, automatically.

An f-string is a way to build text in Python by putting a value inside curly braces, and Python fills it in automatically. Writing `name = "Sam"` and then `f"Hello, {name}!"` produces the text "Hello, Sam!". It is called an f-string because you write a lowercase f right before the opening quote, which tells Python to look inside the braces for things to fill in.

An f-string is written as `f"..."` with any Python expression inside curly braces, not just a variable name: `f"speed_lag_{k}"` with k equal to 3 produces the text speed_lag_3, and `f"{3.14159:.2f}"` produces 3.14 using a format spec to control decimal places. They are commonly used to build column names in a loop, like generating speed_lag_0 through speed_lag_3 by looping k from 0 to 3 and writing `f"speed_lag_{k}"` each time. Without the f, the same text would print the literal characters {k} instead of the value of k.

f-strings, added in Python 3.6, are evaluated at run time each time the line executes, and the expression inside the braces can be arbitrarily complex, a function call, an attribute access, even another f-string, not just a bare variable, which is more general than the older percent-style or `.format()` string formatting it mostly replaced. The format spec after a colon controls things like decimal places, alignment, and thousands separators, following the same mini-language as `str.format()`. They fail, or rather misbehave, in one common way: forgetting the f prefix silently produces the literal template text with unfilled braces rather than raising an error, which is a frustrating class of bug to spot by eye.

f-strings are effectively syntactic sugar over `str.format()`, compiled directly into bytecode that evaluates the embedded expressions at the point the string literal appears, which makes them faster than `.format()` or string concatenation for building repeated column names or log messages in a hot loop. Python 3.12 relaxed the grammar further, allowing nested quotes of the same type and multi-line expressions inside the braces, which earlier versions rejected. A subtle correctness issue in ML code specifically is using an f-string to build a column name from a loop variable and then, elsewhere, hardcoding that name as a literal string; the two can drift out of sync if the loop range changes, producing a KeyError far from where the mismatch was introduced. Using f-strings for anything security-sensitive, like building a SQL query from user input, is a known anti-pattern, since it invites injection; parameterized queries exist for exactly this reason.

In production code, f-strings used to name generated features, as in `f"speed_lag_{k}"`, are convenient but implicit: the set of expected column names exists only as whatever the loop happened to produce, with nothing enforcing that training and serving code generate the identical set, a real and recurring source of train and serve skew in feature pipelines. Mature feature pipelines address this by making the naming scheme an explicit, tested contract, a schema or a shared feature-definition module, rather than trusting that two independent f-string loops elsewhere in the codebase stay in sync. This is a small instance of a broader production pattern: string-based conventions are cheap during prototyping and a recurring source of subtle bugs once a pipeline has more than one place that needs to agree on a name.

target.def: The column the model tries to predict. Here 1 if the station is inside a slow episode h minutes later, else 0.
levels: The target is the answer the model is trying to guess, like when you play a guessing game and someone checks your answer against the real one. Here, the game is guessing whether the road will be slow in half an hour.

The target, also called the label, is the column in your data that holds the correct answer for each row, the thing you are trying to predict, not something you feed into the model as a clue. In this course, the target is 1 if a station is inside a slow-traffic episode h minutes in the future, and 0 if it is not. Everything else in the row, past speed, time of day, and so on, is a feature, a clue, not the answer.

The target column is built by looking ahead: for a row at time t, the label is 1 if the station's speed h minutes later, say 30, falls below the slow threshold, and 0 otherwise, which in pandas means shifting a was-it-slow indicator backward in time relative to the features, effectively `df["target"] = df["is_slow"].shift(-6)` at 5-minute steps for a 30-minute horizon. This makes the target a genuinely future value relative to the row's other columns, so building it correctly requires care not to accidentally include information from the target's own time or later in the features. A model is trained to predict this column from the other columns, and evaluated by how well its predictions on held-out rows match the true target values.

The target here is a relative label, meaning slow is defined relative to that station's own typical speed rather than an absolute speed cutoff, because a state highway's normal speed and a local arterial's normal speed differ enough that one fixed threshold would mislabel one or the other. Choosing the target this way is a modeling decision as consequential as the choice of algorithm: too strict a threshold makes slow episodes rare and the problem heavily imbalanced, and too loose a threshold makes slow nearly meaningless. Constructing the target requires shifting label information into the past relative to features, and getting the sign or shift amount wrong is a common and serious bug, since it can silently create a target that either leaks future information into the features or predicts the wrong horizon entirely. The target's exact definition, the threshold, the horizon, whether it is a point-in-time label or an any-time-within-the-next-h-minutes label, determines what question the whole downstream model actually answers.

A binary in-a-slow-episode-or-not target discards information a regression on raw future speed would keep, a genuine tradeoff: classification gives interpretable probabilities and handles the imbalance-fighting toolkit well, but a continuous speed target could support a richer notion of severity. Label leakage around target construction is the most consequential mistake in this kind of project: any feature computed with a window that reaches even slightly past the label's own time horizon, a centered rolling average, for instance, will make an offline model look far better than it can perform in real deployment, because at serving time those future values do not exist yet. The horizon, 30 minutes here, is itself a hyperparameter with real consequences; shorter horizons are easier to predict but less actionable, longer horizons are more actionable but harder to predict, and multi-task models that predict several horizons at once are one way to avoid committing to just one. Class imbalance in the target, slow episodes are the minority class, means accuracy is a misleading headline metric, and the target's rarity should drive the choice of loss weighting or resampling, not be treated as a detail to handle after the fact.

In production forecasting systems, the target definition is rarely fixed once and left alone; it evolves as stakeholders discover that slow or the chosen horizon does not match what they actually need to act on, which means the labeling logic itself needs the same versioning and review as the model code, since a silent change in how the target is computed invalidates comparisons against past model versions. Multi-horizon, multi-definition targets, several thresholds, several horizons, sometimes a continuous severity score alongside the binary label, are common in mature systems specifically so that different downstream consumers of the prediction do not have to negotiate over a single label. The open research question connecting to the target's definition is causal: today's target only captures whether traffic will be slow, not why, and a target or auxiliary task tied to identifiable causes, an incident, an event, weather, is more useful for a system meant to inform action rather than just alert.

cyclic-encoding.def: Placing a time on a circle with sine and cosine so 23:55 and 00:05 are close.
levels: Think of a clock face. 11:55 at night and 12:05 just after midnight are right next to each other on the clock, even though as plain numbers 2355 and 5 look nothing alike. Cyclic encoding is a trick that makes the computer see time the way a clock does, as a circle, not a straight line of numbers.

If you just wrote time of day as a number of minutes since midnight, 23:55, minute 1435, and 00:05, minute 5, would look almost as far apart as two numbers can be, even though only 10 minutes separate them in real life. Cyclic encoding fixes this by turning the time into a point on a circle using sine and cosine, so that times close together on a clock stay close together as numbers, no matter where midnight falls.

Given a value that repeats, like hour-of-day, first convert it to an angle: angle equals 2π times hour divided by 24. Then create two features: sin(angle) and cos(angle). Midnight, hour 0, and just before midnight, hour 23.9, now land at nearly the same sin-cos point on the unit circle, instead of at opposite ends of a 0-to-23 number line. The same trick applies to day-of-week, period 7, or day-of-year, period 365.

Cyclic encoding turns a periodic variable into a pair of coordinates on the unit circle, which preserves the true circular distance between any two times as ordinary Euclidean distance between their sin-cos points, something a raw integer encoding or even one-hot encoding of hour does not give a model for free. It requires knowing the period in advance, 24 for hour, 7 for day-of-week, and using the wrong period silently produces a broken, non-cyclic mapping. It matters most for models that treat features as ordered or distance-based in a naive way, linear models and neural networks benefit clearly, while tree-based models like LightGBM can partly recover cyclic structure on their own by learning a threshold-based split near midnight, so the encoding helps them less, though it rarely hurts.

Using sin and cos together, rather than either alone, is necessary because a single sine value is not invertible; sin of 30 degrees and sin of 150 degrees are equal, so one feature alone cannot distinguish those two times, while the pair sin-cos is a bijection onto the circle and resolves the ambiguity. A subtlety practitioners often miss is that cyclic encoding assumes the underlying relationship really is smoothly periodic, a reasonable assumption for hour-of-day traffic patterns but a poor one for something like day-of-week, where weekday and weekend behavior can differ sharply rather than blend smoothly across the boundary; in that case, a categorical encoding of day-type may serve better than treating it as continuous and cyclic. Tree models split on a single feature's threshold at a time, so sin and cos features interact only through multiple sequential splits, which can make trees slower to discover cyclic structure than a linear or neural model would, even though trees do not strictly need the encoding to eventually get there.

At production scale, cyclic encoding is a small piece of a larger feature-engineering pattern, Fourier or spectral encodings of time, used more elaborately in industrial forecasting systems, sometimes with multiple harmonics to capture non-sinusoidal periodic shapes like a sharp morning commute spike that a single sine wave fits poorly. An open question in more modern forecasting architectures, transformers, temporal models, is whether learned time embeddings, trained end-to-end rather than hand-specified as sine and cosine, capture this structure better in practice; empirically the answer often depends on how much data is available to learn the embedding from scratch versus how well the hand-built cyclic prior generalizes with limited data.

brier-score.def: Mean squared difference between predicted probability and outcome; lower is better.
levels: Imagine guessing how likely it is to rain, like a 70 percent chance of rain, and then checking how close your guess was to what actually happened. The Brier score is a way to grade those percentage guesses; the closer your guesses are to reality, the lower, and better, your score.

The Brier score measures how good a probability prediction is, by squaring the difference between the predicted probability and the actual outcome, 1 if it happened, 0 if it did not, and averaging that over every prediction. If you predict 90 percent and it happens, your error for that prediction is small, 0.1 squared; if you predict 90 percent and it does not happen, your error is large, 0.9 squared. A perfect predictor has a Brier score of 0; a model that is confidently wrong a lot has a high Brier score.

The formula for one prediction is (p minus y) squared, where p is the predicted probability and y is the actual outcome, 0 or 1; the Brier score is the average of this over all predictions. It ranges from 0, perfect, to 1, perfectly wrong every time, and always predicting the base rate gives a baseline score to compare against. Unlike accuracy, it rewards a model for saying I am not sure, predicting near 0.5, when it genuinely is not sure, rather than forcing an overconfident guess.

The Brier score decomposes into calibration, how close predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, and refinement or resolution, how much the predictions vary and separate the classes, which is why two models can have similar Brier scores for very different reasons, one well-calibrated but not very discriminating, another sharp but poorly calibrated. It is a strictly proper scoring rule, meaning a forecaster who truly believes the outcome has probability p minimizes their expected Brier score by reporting p honestly, rather than by hedging toward 0.5 or rounding toward 0 or 1, a real mathematical property, not just a convenient interpretation. It generalizes log loss's goal of penalizing confident wrong answers, but with a bounded, squared penalty rather than log loss's unbounded one, which makes it less sensitive to a single very confident wrong prediction. It fails to be very informative on its own when class imbalance is severe, since a trivial always-predict-the-base-rate model can already achieve a fairly low Brier score, so it should be compared to that baseline, not read as an absolute number.

The calibration-refinement decomposition, sometimes called the Murphy decomposition, lets you diagnose why a model's Brier score is what it is: a reliability diagram visualizes the calibration component directly, and a model with excellent AUC but poor calibration can still have a mediocre Brier score, surprising practitioners who expected the two metrics to agree. Brier score and log loss usually rank models similarly but not always identically, because log loss's unbounded penalty for confident wrong predictions makes it far more sensitive to rare, badly miscalibrated extreme predictions than the bounded, squared Brier penalty is. A common practitioner mistake is comparing Brier scores across datasets or across different class balances as if the number were an absolute quality measure, when it should always be compared against the Brier score of the trivial base-rate predictor on that same dataset. Post-hoc calibration methods, Platt scaling, isotonic regression, are typically evaluated by how much they improve Brier score or log loss on a held-out set without hurting AUC, which is the standard way to check that recalibration is fixing probabilities rather than distorting them.

In production systems where a probability is shown to a person or feeds into a downstream decision, routing, alerting, resource allocation, Brier score is often tracked in production monitoring, not just at training time, because calibration can drift after deployment even when discrimination, AUC, stays stable, and Brier score is sensitive to exactly that kind of drift. Multi-class and multi-label generalizations of Brier score exist and are used when a system outputs a full distribution over more than two outcomes, not just a single slow or not-slow probability. An open practical problem is that Brier score treats all miscalibration equally regardless of the cost of being wrong at different operating points, so production systems often complement it with cost-weighted or threshold-specific metrics tied to the actual downstream decision the probability feeds into.

sigmoid.def: 1 / (1 + e^(−z)): turns any number into a value between 0 and 1.
levels: Imagine a dimmer switch for a light: no matter how hard you push it, the light can never get brighter than fully on or dimmer than fully off. Sigmoid is a math dimmer switch; it takes any number, even a huge one, and squeezes it down to somewhere between 0 and 1.

Sigmoid is a function that takes any number, positive or negative, huge or tiny, and turns it into a value between 0 and 1. Very negative numbers become close to 0, very positive numbers become close to 1, and 0 becomes exactly 0.5. This is useful because a probability has to be between 0 and 1, so sigmoid is how a model turns a raw score into something that can be read as the chance this is true.

The formula is sigmoid(z) equals 1 divided by (1 plus e to the power of negative z), where e is Euler's number, about 2.718, and z can be any real number. Plugging in z equals 0 gives exactly 0.5; large positive z pushes the output toward 1, large negative z pushes it toward 0. In logistic regression, z is a weighted sum of the features, z equals w1x1 plus w2x2 plus more plus b, and sigmoid(z) turns that weighted sum into the predicted probability that the label is 1.

Sigmoid is the inverse of the logit function, the log of p divided by (1 minus p), which is why logistic regression is sometimes described as modeling the log-odds as a linear function of the features and then mapping back to a probability with sigmoid. Its derivative has a convenient closed form, sigmoid(z) times (1 minus sigmoid(z)), which is why it was historically popular as a neural network activation function; the gradient is cheap to compute directly from the function's own output. It saturates for large magnitude z: the derivative approaches 0 as z moves far from 0 in either direction, which means gradient-based learning slows to a crawl exactly where the function is most confident, a problem known as vanishing gradients. This is why modern deep networks mostly use ReLU in hidden layers, reserving sigmoid for the final layer of a binary classifier, where its output is genuinely meant to be read as a probability.

The vanishing-gradient problem compounds across layers in a deep network; each sigmoid layer multiplies gradients by a factor bounded by 0.25, the maximum of sigmoid's derivative, so a network with many sigmoid layers can have gradients shrink toward zero by the time they reach early layers, which was a major obstacle to training deep networks before ReLU and better initialization schemes became standard. Sigmoid combined with the wrong loss, mean squared error, say, instead of cross-entropy, produces a particularly bad combination: the loss landscape becomes non-convex and gradients saturate even more, part of why cross-entropy loss is paired with sigmoid almost universally in practice, not by convention alone but because the combination has a clean, well-behaved gradient, predicted probability minus true label. For multi-class problems, sigmoid generalizes to softmax when classes are mutually exclusive, but sigmoid applied independently per class is the right choice instead when labels are not mutually exclusive, multi-label problems, a distinction practitioners sometimes get backwards.

In production systems, sigmoid is nearly always the final output layer for a binary probability, even in architectures that use very different machinery internally to compute z, because downstream consumers of the model, alerting thresholds, calibration checks, ranking, expect a genuine probability, not an arbitrary score. Numerical stability matters more in production code than the math suggests: naively computing e to the power of negative z for very negative or very positive z overflows or underflows in floating point, so production implementations use numerically stable formulations rather than the textbook formula directly. An ongoing practical concern at scale is that a network's raw sigmoid outputs are often poorly calibrated as probabilities even when the ranking is accurate, so production systems frequently add a calibration layer after training rather than trusting the sigmoid output directly as a decision-ready probability.

regularization.def: Any penalty or constraint that keeps a model from fitting noise: weight decay, leaf limits, feature and row subsampling, early stopping.
levels: If you let a kid memorize the answers to last year's test instead of learning the subject, they will do great on that exact test and terribly on a new one. Regularization is a rule that stops a model from memorizing every little detail of its practice questions, so it actually learns the general idea instead.

Regularization is anything you add to how a model learns that stops it from fitting every tiny wiggle in the training data too closely, which usually makes it worse on new data it has not seen. One common form is a penalty added to the training goal that discourages very large weights, since huge weights are often a sign a model has bent itself to match noise rather than a real pattern. Another form is simply stopping training early, before the model has had a chance to overfit, or limiting how complicated a decision tree is allowed to get.

In linear and logistic regression, L2 regularization, also called ridge, or weight decay, adds lambda times the sum of squared weights to the loss function being minimized, where lambda controls how strongly large weights are punished; a bigger lambda means simpler, smaller weights and less risk of overfitting, but too big a lambda underfits. L1 regularization adds lambda times the sum of absolute weights instead, which tends to push some weights to exactly zero, effectively doing feature selection. For tree-based models like LightGBM, regularization takes different forms: limiting the number of leaves per tree, requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf, and randomly subsampling rows or features for each tree, all of which stop any single tree from fitting the training data too exactly.

L2 regularization has a clean Bayesian interpretation: it corresponds to putting a Gaussian prior on the weights and finding the maximum a posteriori estimate rather than the plain maximum likelihood estimate, so regularization strength lambda is directly tied to how confident that prior is that weights should be small. Early stopping regularizes implicitly, without an explicit penalty term, by simply not letting gradient descent run long enough to fit noise; this makes the number of training iterations itself a regularization hyperparameter, tuned on a validation set exactly like lambda would be. In tree ensembles, subsampling rows and features per split regularizes by decorrelating individual trees' mistakes, so their errors average out rather than compound. It fails to help, and can actively hurt, when the model was already underfitting, too simple to capture the real pattern; adding more regularization on top of underfitting only makes the model worse, so the fix in that case is a more expressive model or better features, not stronger regularization.

The bias-variance tradeoff is the formal frame: regularization trades a small increase in bias, the model is now slightly wrong about the training data on purpose, for a larger decrease in variance, the model is far less sensitive to which particular training sample it happened to see, and the right amount of regularization is whatever minimizes their sum on held-out data, found by tuning lambda, or leaf count, or early-stopping patience, via cross-validation rather than guessing. A common misconception is treating regularization as free protection against overfitting that can be cranked up without cost; in reality every regularization method has an implicit assumption about what simple means, small weights, few leaves, sparse features, and if that assumption does not match the true underlying pattern, regularization introduces its own systematic bias. Modern deep learning also gets substantial implicit regularization from SGD's own noise and from the choice of learning rate and batch size, not just from explicit penalty terms, part of why very large neural networks can generalize well despite having far more parameters than training examples, a phenomenon still not fully explained by classical bias-variance theory. Dropout, data augmentation, and ensembling are all regularization in the broad sense, anything that reduces a model's tendency to fit training-set-specific noise, even though they do not look like a penalty term added to a loss function.

At scale, the practical question shifts from how strong should the penalty be to which combination of implicit and explicit regularizers, at what settings, transfers across a fleet of related models trained on different slices of data, since retuning every regularization hyperparameter from scratch for every model in a production system is often infeasible, and defaults tuned on one distribution can be quietly wrong for another. Double descent, the empirical observation that very over-parameterized models can generalize well again after initially getting worse as capacity increases past the classical sweet spot, has complicated the textbook bias-variance story and remains an active research question about why some large models seem to need less explicit regularization than classical theory would predict. In production, regularization choices interact with fairness and robustness goals in ways classical theory does not address: a model regularized purely to minimize average validation error can still learn to under-serve a minority slice of the data, a separate concern from the variance-reduction regularization is classically meant to solve.

relu.def: max(z, 0): zeroes negatives. The nonlinearity that lets a network bend.
levels: Imagine a wall with a ramp: if you're already above the ground, you keep going up exactly as much as you pushed, but if you try to go below the ground, the wall just stops you flat at zero. ReLU does that to numbers; positive numbers pass right through, and any negative number becomes zero.

ReLU stands for rectified linear unit, and it is a simple rule: if the number is positive, keep it exactly as it is; if the number is negative, turn it into zero. A neural network computes a weighted sum of its inputs, and then ReLU decides which of those sums turn on, stay positive, and which get shut off to zero. This small bend is what lets a network learn shapes more complicated than a straight line.

The formula is ReLU(z) equals max(z, 0): if z is 5, ReLU(z) is 5; if z is negative 3, ReLU(z) is 0. In a neural network layer, you first compute z, a weighted sum of the inputs plus a bias, then apply ReLU to get the layer's output, which becomes the next layer's input. Without a nonlinear function like ReLU between layers, stacking multiple layers would mathematically collapse into one single linear layer, no matter how many layers you stacked, because a linear function of a linear function is still linear.

ReLU's derivative is 1 for z greater than 0 and 0 for z less than 0, undefined exactly at z equals 0, conventionally set to 0 or 1 in practice, which is much cheaper to compute than sigmoid's derivative and, crucially, does not shrink toward zero for large positive z, which is why ReLU networks train faster and avoid much of the vanishing-gradient problem that plagued deep sigmoid networks. Its main failure mode is the dying ReLU problem: if a unit's weights update such that its input is always negative across the training data, its output and gradient are permanently zero, and that unit stops learning entirely for the rest of training. Variants like Leaky ReLU, a small nonzero slope for negative z, and ELU exist specifically to address this by letting a small gradient flow even for negative inputs. ReLU networks are not differentiable everywhere, the kink at zero, but in practice this almost never matters for optimization, since landing exactly on zero has probability essentially zero during real training.

The dying ReLU problem interacts with initialization and learning rate: a learning rate that is too high can push many units into the permanently-negative regime in the first few steps of training, part of why initialization schemes tuned for ReLU networks and careful learning-rate warmup matter more for ReLU networks than the activation function's simplicity might suggest. GELU and Swish, smooth approximations to ReLU used in transformers and other modern architectures, trade ReLU's cheap computation and hard zero for a small but empirically consistent improvement in performance on large models, though the underlying reason is still not fully settled beyond smoother gradients seem to help optimization at scale. A common misconception is that ReLU's nonlinearity is what makes deep learning powerful in some deep theoretical sense; in fact almost any nonlinearity between layers restores the network's ability to represent nonlinear functions, and ReLU's popularity is mostly about optimization behavior, fast, sparse, well-behaved gradients, rather than representational power specifically. ReLU also induces sparsity, roughly half of a randomly initialized network's ReLU units are inactive for a typical input, which some researchers view as a useful inductive bias and others view as wasted capacity, and the tradeoff is still debated.

At production scale, the choice of activation function is one of the more thoroughly explored architecture hyperparameters, and different families of models have settled on different defaults for reasons that are partly empirical and partly about matching hardware; GELU-family activations dominate in transformers, while ReLU and its cheap variants remain common in latency-sensitive on-device models, in part because ReLU is trivial to implement efficiently in low-precision, quantized inference on mobile or embedded hardware. An open research question is why smooth activations consistently edge out ReLU on large-scale pretraining tasks despite ReLU's clean theoretical simplicity, since the standard vanishing and dying-unit explanations do not fully account for the gap. On-device and hardware-constrained deployment often specifically favors ReLU precisely because it composes well with quantization, its output range and sparsity are cheap to represent in low bit-widths, even when a smoother activation would train to marginally better accuracy, making activation choice one of the places accuracy and deployment cost trade off directly.

multi-task.def: One model with several outputs, here the three horizons.
levels: Imagine one friend who can answer three of your questions at once instead of you asking three different friends. A multi-task model is like that: one model that gives you several answers, will it be slow in 15, 30, and 60 minutes, all from the same brain.

Multi-task means training a single model to predict more than one thing at the same time, instead of training a separate model for each prediction. In this course, one model predicts whether a station will be slow in 15 minutes, in 30 minutes, and in 60 minutes, all at once, rather than needing three completely separate models. The model shares most of its internal computation across the three predictions and only splits into separate outputs at the very end.

A multi-task neural network shares hidden layers, the parts that learn general patterns from the input, across all tasks, then has a separate small output layer, or head, for each task. For three horizons, the final layer might be `nn.Linear(hidden_size, 3)`, turning one shared internal representation into three separate numbers, logits, one per horizon, each then passed through sigmoid to get a probability. The training loss is usually the sum, or a weighted sum, of the loss for each task, so a single backward pass updates the shared layers using information from all three predictions at once.

Multi-task learning works when the tasks are related enough that learning one helps the others; here, the three horizons share almost all of the same underlying physics, how traffic at a station evolves, so a representation useful for predicting 30 minutes ahead is largely useful for 15 and 60 minutes too. This acts as an implicit regularizer: a shared representation trained on three related signals is less likely to overfit to noise specific to any one horizon than three separate models trained independently would be, especially when data for any single horizon is limited. It fails, or at least stops helping, when tasks are not actually related, or when one task's gradient signal is much larger than another's and dominates the shared layers during training, effectively starving the smaller task of useful updates unless the loss is reweighted. Choosing how to weight each task's loss in the sum is itself a real design decision, not an afterthought, since an unweighted sum implicitly favors whichever task has a naturally larger loss scale.

Task weighting is a genuinely hard subproblem; fixed weights chosen by hand are brittle across datasets, and more principled approaches, uncertainty-weighted losses, gradient normalization schemes, or dynamically adjusting weights during training, exist specifically because naive equal weighting often lets an easy task dominate a shared representation at a harder task's expense. Negative transfer is the central risk: when tasks are less related than assumed, forcing a shared representation can make every task's performance worse than training separate single-task models would, the opposite of the intended benefit and genuinely hard to predict in advance without trying both. Architecture choice matters too; how much of the network is shared versus task-specific is a spectrum, from almost everything shared with tiny per-task heads, as in this course's 3-horizon setup, to mostly separate networks that share only early layers, and the right point on that spectrum depends on how similar the tasks really are. A subtlety practitioners often get wrong is evaluating a multi-task model only on its combined loss rather than checking each task's individual metric separately, which can hide a case where two tasks improved and one quietly got worse than its single-task baseline.

In production systems, multi-task models are attractive beyond pure accuracy because they reduce serving cost; one forward pass produces several predictions instead of running several separate models, which matters a great deal at scale where inference cost is a real budget line, not just an accuracy metric. Large multi-task and multi-domain models are an active area where the central open problem is the same negative-transfer question from the research literature, just at much larger scale and with much higher cost to diagnosing it, since retraining a huge shared model to test whether one task is hurting another is expensive. Mixture-of-experts architectures are a modern industrial answer to this tension, letting different tasks or inputs route to different subsets of a large shared network's parameters instead of forcing every task through exactly the same shared layers, which softens the sharing-versus-specialization tradeoff instead of resolving it by hand-picked architecture.

median.def: The middle value when all the numbers are lined up in order; half the values are above it and half below.
levels: If you line up everyone in your class from shortest to tallest and pick the person standing exactly in the middle, that person's height is the median. It does not care how short the shortest person is or how tall the tallest is, just who is in the middle.

The median is the middle value of a list of numbers once you sort them from smallest to largest. If there are an odd number of values, it is the exact middle one; if there are an even number, it is the average of the two middle ones. Unlike the average, or mean, the median is not pulled around by one extremely large or small number, which is why it is often used to describe typical income or typical commute time.

To find the median of a sorted list of n numbers: if n is odd, it is the value at position (n plus 1) divided by 2; if n is even, it is the average of the values at positions n over 2 and n over 2 plus 1. In pandas, `df["speed"].median()` computes it directly. Compared to the mean, the median resists outliers: adding one absurdly slow reading, a crash, a closed lane, barely moves the median but can shift the mean a lot, which is why median speed is often a more robust summary of typical traffic than mean speed.

Formally, the median is the 50th percentile, the value below which half the data falls and above which the other half falls, and it minimizes the sum of absolute deviations from itself, the way the mean minimizes the sum of squared deviations, exactly why the median is less sensitive to extreme values, squaring in the mean's objective punishes large deviations far more than the linear penalty the median's objective uses. Computing an exact median naively requires sorting the data, though selection algorithms can find it in expected linear time without a full sort. For a symmetric distribution, mean and median coincide; for a skewed one, like commute times, which have a long tail of very slow trips, they diverge, and reporting only the mean can misleadingly suggest a typical trip is worse than most people's actual experience. It fails to summarize a distribution completely on its own; two datasets with the same median can have very different spreads or shapes, so it is typically reported alongside percentiles or the interquartile range, not alone.

The median is a special case of an L-estimator and connects to quantile regression, which generalizes predict the median to predict any percentile of the conditional distribution, useful in traffic forecasting when you care about, say, the 90th-percentile delay rather than just the typical one. Its robustness comes at a statistical efficiency cost: for data that really is close to normally distributed, the mean is a more efficient estimator, lower variance across samples, than the median, so preferring the median purely for robustness is a real tradeoff, not a free upgrade. A practitioner mistake is using the median as a drop-in replacement for the mean everywhere without checking whether the loss of information, the median ignores the actual magnitude of values above and below it, only their rank, matters for the downstream use; for imputing a single missing sensor reading, the median of nearby readings is usually a fine choice, but for a quantity where the total matters, total flow, not typical speed, a median-based summary is the wrong tool. The median is also non-differentiable as a function of the data in a way that complicates using it directly inside a gradient-based loss function, part of why the closely related but smooth pinball, or quantile, loss is used instead when a model needs to learn to predict a median or other quantile.

In production monitoring, the median, often as p50, is a standard robustness-preferring summary statistic for latency, sensor readings, and model errors specifically because production data reliably contains outliers, a stuck sensor, a network blip, that would distort a mean-based dashboard, so median and percentile-based reporting is closer to the industry default than the mean is. Streaming and approximate median algorithms exist because computing an exact median requires holding or sorting the full dataset, which is infeasible at the volume and velocity of real production telemetry, so production systems trade a small, bounded approximation error for the ability to track medians and percentiles continuously over huge, unbounded streams.

bayesian.def: Updating a belief, the prior, with new evidence via the data's likelihood, producing an updated belief, the posterior; Bayes' rule links the three.
levels: Imagine you think it might rain today, so you bring an umbrella just in case, that's your first guess. Then you look outside and see dark clouds, so you become more sure it will rain. Bayesian thinking is exactly that: starting with a guess, then updating it once you see new clues.

In Bayesian thinking, you start with a prior: your best guess about something before you have new evidence, like there's usually a 30 percent chance of a slow commute on any given day. Then you see new evidence, like today's weather or an accident report, and combine it with your prior belief to get a posterior: an updated guess that takes both your starting belief and the new evidence into account. Bayes' rule is the exact math formula for combining a prior with evidence to get the posterior.

Bayes' rule states: posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood, or more fully, the probability of A given B equals the probability of B given A, times the probability of A, divided by the probability of B, where the probability of A is the prior probability of A, the probability of B given A is the likelihood of seeing evidence B if A is true, and the probability of A given B is the posterior probability of A after seeing B. For example, if the prior chance of a slow commute is 30 percent, and seeing an accident report makes a slow commute much more likely, a high likelihood, Bayes' rule tells you exactly how much to raise your estimate, rather than just guessing more likely.

A Bayesian treats unknown quantities, a model's parameters, or the probability of a slow commute, as random variables with a probability distribution representing belief, and updates that distribution using observed data via Bayes' rule, in contrast to a frequentist approach, which treats the true parameter as a fixed unknown number and reasons instead about the long-run behavior of an estimator across repeated samples. The prior encodes assumptions or existing knowledge before seeing data, the likelihood is how probable the observed data is under different parameter values, and the posterior combines both into a full distribution over what the parameter or prediction could be, rather than a single point estimate. This full posterior distribution is what gives Bayesian methods a natural notion of uncertainty, a narrow posterior means confident, a wide one means uncertain, that a plain point-estimate model does not automatically provide. It fails to be tractable in closed form for most realistic models, which is why practical Bayesian inference usually relies on approximation methods, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, rather than the clean formula worked out by hand.

A subtle but important point is that L2 regularization in ordinary logistic or linear regression is mathematically identical to placing a Gaussian prior on the weights and finding the maximum a posteriori point estimate, not the full posterior; MAP is a Bayesian-flavored shortcut that gives you a single best point rather than the full uncertainty a genuinely Bayesian treatment would provide, and conflating the two is a common misconception. The choice of prior is a real modeling decision with consequences, not a formality: an overly informative prior can dominate a small dataset's evidence and bias the posterior toward the prior's assumptions, while an overly vague prior can make inference computationally unstable or slow to concentrate even with plenty of data. Bayesian model comparison, via marginal likelihood, or Bayes factors, offers a principled alternative to cross-validation for choosing between models, but the marginal likelihood is notoriously sensitive to prior choice in ways that can make model comparison misleading if priors are not chosen carefully. Modern Bayesian deep learning exists specifically to bring calibrated uncertainty to models that are otherwise pure point-estimators, since a plain neural network's sigmoid output is not automatically well-calibrated as true uncertainty in the Bayesian sense.

In production systems, full Bayesian inference is often too expensive to run at prediction-serving latency, so practical uncertainty estimates at scale usually come from cheaper approximations, deep ensembles, Monte Carlo dropout, or simple calibration layers, that behave somewhat like a Bayesian posterior without doing the actual integration Bayes' rule calls for. Bayesian ideas remain central conceptually even where the machinery is approximated: online learning systems that update a model's beliefs as new data streams in, A/B testing frameworks that use Bayesian methods to make sequential decisions with less data than frequentist significance testing requires, and recommendation systems balancing exploration and exploitation are all explicitly Bayesian in framing. An open, practically important question is how to get calibrated, genuinely useful uncertainty estimates out of very large models cheaply enough to serve them at scale, since the field still lacks a cheap, reliable substitute for the full posterior that scales to billion-parameter models.

kl-divergence.def: A number measuring how different one probability distribution is from another; zero only when they match exactly, and it is not symmetric.
levels: Imagine you have a map of where you think your friends usually stand at recess, and then you actually go count where they are standing. KL divergence is a number that says how wrong your map was; the more your guess differs from reality, the bigger the number.

KL divergence measures how different one probability distribution is from another one. If you predict there is a 90 percent chance of one outcome and a 10 percent chance of another, but the real world is actually 50-50, KL divergence gives you a number showing how far off your guess was. A KL divergence of zero means your predicted distribution matches the real one exactly; the further apart they are, the bigger the number gets.

The formula for comparing a true distribution P to a predicted distribution Q is the sum over every possible outcome x of P(x) times the log of P(x) divided by Q(x). It is always zero or positive, and exactly zero only when P and Q are identical. It is not symmetric: the KL divergence from P to Q is generally not equal to the KL divergence from Q to P, so it measures a direction of difference, not a plain distance between the two distributions.

KL divergence is closely tied to cross-entropy: the cross-entropy between P and Q equals the true distribution's own entropy plus the KL divergence from P to Q, so minimizing cross-entropy loss during training, what almost every classifier actually does, is mathematically equivalent to minimizing KL divergence between the true label distribution and the model's predicted distribution, since the true distribution's entropy does not depend on the model's parameters and can be ignored during optimization. It is always non-negative, a consequence of Jensen's inequality applied to the log function, and equals zero exactly when the two distributions are identical almost everywhere, which is what makes it usable as a loss to minimize. Its asymmetry matters practically: KL from P to Q, used as a training loss where P is the true data distribution, penalizes the model heavily for assigning near-zero probability to outcomes that actually happen, Q must cover P, while KL from Q to P used the other way around penalizes differently, favoring a model that avoids assigning high probability to outcomes that do not happen; the choice of direction changes what kind of mistake gets penalized most. It fails to be a true distance metric because of that asymmetry and because it does not satisfy the triangle inequality, so calling it a distance between distributions, while common shorthand, is mathematically loose.

The asymmetry has real practical consequences beyond training classifiers: in variational inference, minimizing KL from Q to P where Q is a tractable approximation and P is an intractable true posterior tends to produce mode-seeking behavior, Q concentrates on one mode of P and ignores others, whereas minimizing KL from P to Q tends to be mode-covering, Q spreads out to cover all of P's mass, and choosing the wrong direction for a given application produces systematically wrong-shaped approximations. In reinforcement learning and generative modeling, KL divergence terms appear explicitly as regularizers, for instance keeping an updated policy close to a reference policy, or keeping a learned latent distribution close to a prior in a variational autoencoder, where the direction and weighting of the KL term is a genuine design choice with real behavioral consequences, not a mathematical footnote. A common misconception is treating small KL divergence as automatically meaning the two distributions are similar in every way that matters; KL divergence can be dominated by disagreement on a single low-probability outcome, if Q assigns it near-zero probability while P does not, the log ratio blows up, which can make it a poor practical similarity measure when P has long tails. Mutual information, used for feature selection, is itself a KL divergence, specifically the KL divergence between a joint distribution and the product of its marginals, which is why entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, and mutual information are usually taught together as one connected family of ideas.

At production and research scale, KL divergence terms show up as regularizers almost everywhere generative or probabilistic modeling is involved; reinforcement learning from human feedback keeps a fine-tuned language model's policy close to its starting policy via a KL penalty specifically to prevent the fine-tuned model from drifting into degenerate, reward-hacking behavior, and this KL penalty's weight is one of the most sensitive hyperparameters in that whole training pipeline. Estimating KL divergence from samples rather than known distributions is itself a hard, actively researched problem, especially in high dimensions, where naive estimators are badly biased with limited data, a real obstacle in evaluating and comparing large generative models where the true underlying distribution is never known in closed form. An open question tying back to this course's classifier is whether KL-based training objectives, tuned mainly for average-case log-likelihood, are the right objective at all for applications, like flagging rare slow-traffic episodes, that care disproportionately about tail behavior the average KL divergence can underweight.

cross-validation.def: Splitting data into several train and test folds and averaging performance across them, to estimate how a model will do on unseen data.
levels: Imagine practicing a spelling test with your friends taking turns being the teacher who checks your work, so you get checked several different times instead of just once. Cross-validation is like that for a model: it gets tested several different times on different parts of the data, so you get a fairer sense of how good it really is.

Cross-validation is a way to test a model more thoroughly than a single train and test split. You split the data into several equal parts, called folds, then train the model on all but one fold and test it on the one left out, repeating this so every fold gets a turn being the test set. Averaging the scores from all those rounds gives a more trustworthy estimate of how well the model will do on data it has never seen, since it is not relying on just one lucky or unlucky split.

In k-fold cross-validation, the data is split into k equal parts, commonly 5 or 10; the model trains on k minus 1 folds and tests on the remaining one, k times total, once per fold, and the k test scores are averaged. In scikit-learn, `cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)` does this automatically.
