For time-series data like the traffic dataset here, ordinary random-fold cross-validation is wrong, because it can train on future data and test on the past; `TimeSeriesSplit` instead uses only earlier data to train and later data to test in each fold, respecting the arrow of time.

The purpose of cross-validation is to get a lower-variance, more reliable estimate of a model's out-of-sample performance than a single train and test split provides, and to do so using every row of data for both training and testing, just never the same row for both at once, which matters especially when data is limited. It is also the standard way to choose hyperparameters, like lambda in regularized regression, or LightGBM's leaf count: try several settings, cross-validate each, and pick the one with the best average validation score, ideally using a separate held-out test set afterward that was never touched during that selection process. `TimeSeriesSplit` is necessary here specifically because ordinary shuffled k-fold cross-validation leaks information: a model trained partly on data from after the test period, even indirectly through nearby time-correlated rows, will report unrealistically good scores that will not hold up once deployed on genuinely future data. It fails, or rather overstates performance, whenever there is any dependency between rows that a random shuffle destroys and the real deployment setting does not, common in time series, grouped data, all rows from one station leaking into both train and test, and other settings where the rows-are-independent assumption is quietly violated.

Choosing the right cross-validation scheme is itself a modeling decision as important as choosing the model: for this course's traffic data, both time, no training on the future, and station identity, whether a station seen at training time should also appear at test time, or whether the model should generalize to unseen stations, are dimensions that can leak if not handled correctly, and a naive `TimeSeriesSplit` alone does not automatically prevent station-level leakage. A frequent misconception is that cross-validation is always better than a single split; for time series specifically, shuffled cross-validation actively produces fantasy scores, so the correct fix is choosing a validation scheme that matches the real deployment setting, not simply adding more folds. Nested cross-validation, an outer loop for performance estimation, an inner loop for hyperparameter selection, exists to avoid the subtler leakage of using the same cross-validation folds both to pick hyperparameters and to report the final performance number, which otherwise produces an optimistic bias even without any time or group leakage. The number of folds trades bias against variance and cost: more folds means each training set is closer to the full dataset, lower bias, but the folds' scores become more correlated with each other and computation grows linearly with k, so 5 or 10 folds is a practical compromise rather than a principled optimum.

In production ML systems, backtesting, cross-validation's real-world analogue for time series, has to account for the fact that a model retrained periodically in production sees a moving window of recent data, so evaluation protocols need to simulate that retraining cadence, rolling-origin evaluation, rather than a single static split, to honestly estimate how the deployed system will behave over time. At scale, computing many folds across large datasets and large models is expensive enough that practitioners often substitute a single, carefully chosen time-based holdout for full cross-validation, accepting a noisier estimate in exchange for tractable compute, a real and often underappreciated tradeoff compared to academic settings where compute is not the binding constraint. An open, still-debated question in industrial ML is how to detect when a cross-validated backtest is quietly overstating real-world performance because the deployment environment has drifted from the historical data the backtest was built on, a distribution-shift problem cross-validation, however carefully designed, cannot fully protect against on its own.

sgd.def: Stochastic gradient descent: updating a model's weights using the gradient from a small batch of examples at a time, not the whole dataset.
levels: Imagine you're trying to find the lowest point in a hilly park, but instead of walking around with your eyes closed feeling for the slope everywhere at once, you take one step at a time downhill, checking just a little bit of ground each step. SGD walks downhill toward a better model the same way, one small step at a time.

Gradient descent is how a model learns: it looks at how wrong its current guesses are, figures out which direction to adjust its numbers, weights, to be less wrong, and takes a small step in that direction, over and over. Stochastic means it does this using just a small random batch of examples at a time instead of the entire dataset every single step, which makes each step much faster, even though it is a little noisier and less precise than using everything at once.

The update rule is w, a weight, becomes w minus eta times the gradient, where eta is the learning rate, how big a step to take, and the gradient is computed from a small batch of training examples rather than the full dataset, which is what stochastic refers to. A batch size of, say, 32 or 64 examples is common; using the full dataset every step is called batch gradient descent, and using exactly one example per step is the extreme, noisiest version of SGD. Too large a learning rate causes the loss to bounce around or diverge instead of decreasing; too small a learning rate makes training painfully slow.

SGD's core tradeoff is noise for speed: computing a gradient from a small batch is a noisy, unbiased estimate of the true full-dataset gradient, but it is far cheaper per step, which lets a model take many more, smaller steps in the same amount of time; in practice this usually reaches a good solution faster than fewer, more precise full-batch steps would. For a convex problem like logistic regression, SGD is guaranteed to converge to the global optimum under a properly decaying learning rate schedule, though in practice a well-tuned constant or simple decay schedule is used instead of the theoretically ideal one. Momentum, accumulating a moving average of past gradients before applying the update, and adaptive methods like Adam, which additionally adapt the learning rate per parameter based on recent gradient magnitudes, are refinements of plain SGD meant to speed convergence and reduce sensitivity to the learning rate choice. It fails, or trains poorly, when the learning rate is badly mismatched to the problem, too high diverges, too low stalls, when batches are too small to give a useful gradient estimate for a very noisy loss surface, or when features are on very different numeric scales, which distorts the effective step size differently across parameters.

For a convex loss like logistic regression's, SGD provably reaches the global optimum because the loss surface has no local minima to get stuck in, but for the highly non-convex loss surfaces of deep networks, SGD's noise is itself believed to be part of why it generalizes well; it tends to avoid sharp, narrow minima that fit the training data too exactly, settling instead into flatter minima that are argued, though not fully proven, to generalize better. Adam and other adaptive optimizers converge faster in early training and are less sensitive to learning-rate tuning, but plain SGD with momentum, tuned carefully, often generalizes at least as well or better on the final model for many vision and tabular tasks, a real, somewhat counterintuitive tradeoff practitioners have to weigh rather than always reaching for the fanciest optimizer. Learning-rate schedules, warmup, then decay, cosine annealing, one-cycle policies, matter as much as the choice of optimizer itself, and a fixed learning rate is rarely optimal across an entire training run, since the ideal step size early in training is typically larger than the ideal step size near convergence. Batch size and learning rate are coupled, not independent choices: scaling up batch size without also scaling the learning rate, roughly linearly, up to a point, tends to produce worse generalization even though the gradient estimate itself is less noisy, which surprises practitioners who assume more data per step is strictly better.

At production training scale, SGD's per-step compute cost and its interaction with distributed training, splitting a batch across many GPUs or accelerators, then synchronizing gradients, becomes as important as its statistical convergence properties, and much of large-scale training engineering is about keeping large-batch distributed SGD both fast, well utilized hardware, and stable, not diverging as batch size and learning rate both scale up. Modern large-model training almost universally uses Adam or a close variant rather than plain SGD, largely for optimization speed and robustness on the huge, irregular loss surfaces of transformer models, even though the theoretical understanding of why Adam works so well at that scale remains incomplete. An open research question, directly relevant to why SGD's noise seems to help generalization, is developing a rigorous theory connecting optimizer choice, batch size, and learning rate to the generalization of the specific solution SGD or Adam converges to; the empirical practice at scale has run well ahead of a full theoretical explanation.

embedding.def: A dense vector of numbers, learned from data, that represents a category so similar categories end up close together in that vector space.
levels: Imagine giving every animal a secret set of coordinates on a map, so that cats and lions end up near each other because they're both a bit alike, while cats and fish end up far apart. An embedding is a set of numbers like that for a category, learned so that similar things land close together.

An embedding turns a category, like a station ID or a word, into a list of numbers, a vector, that a model can actually do math with. Instead of just labeling each station with an arbitrary ID number that has no real meaning, station 5 is not more than station 3 in any real sense, an embedding learns numbers for each station such that stations that behave similarly end up with similar number lists. The model learns these numbers itself during training, rather than someone writing them by hand.

An embedding is typically a short vector, say 8 or 16 numbers, one per category, like one vector per station_id, stored in a lookup table that starts out random and gets updated during training just like any other weight in the model. In PyTorch, `nn.Embedding(num_stations, embedding_dim)` creates this lookup table; feeding in a station's ID returns its current embedding vector, which then flows into the rest of the network like any other feature. Stations with genuinely similar traffic behavior tend to end up with similar embedding vectors after training, even though nothing explicitly told the model which stations were alike, that structure is discovered from the data.

Embeddings are the standard way to handle a categorical feature with many possible values in a neural network, replacing one-hot encoding, a huge, mostly-zero vector with one 1 per category, with a compact, dense, learned representation that scales far better as the number of categories grows and lets the model share statistical strength across related categories instead of treating each one as entirely independent. Nearby points in the resulting embedding space tend to reflect meaningful similarity, for station embeddings this might mean stations on the same freeway segment or with similar typical congestion patterns cluster together, which is a byproduct of training on the actual prediction task, not a separately imposed goal. It requires enough data per category to learn a good embedding; a station seen only a handful of times in training gets a poorly estimated, essentially near-random embedding, a real limitation for rare categories, the cold-start problem. It fails to generalize to entirely new categories unseen during training, a brand-new station added after deployment has no learned embedding at all, which typically requires falling back to some default or average embedding until enough new data accumulates.

Embedding dimension is a real hyperparameter with a tradeoff: too small and the embedding cannot capture the true diversity of station behavior, too large and the model has more parameters to overfit with, especially for categories with limited data per category, a rough rule of thumb some practitioners use is scaling embedding dimension with the log or fourth root of the number of categories, though this is a heuristic, not a theorem. Pretrained or transfer-learned embeddings, learning them on a large related task, then reusing or fine-tuning them on a smaller target task, can substantially help the cold-start and limited-data problems, an idea borrowed directly from word embeddings in NLP and widely reused across recommender systems and tabular deep learning. A frequent practitioner mistake is comparing embedding-based neural models against tree-based models using native categorical support and concluding embeddings are unnecessary, when in fact the two approaches handle categorical information via genuinely different mechanisms, trees split on category subsets directly, embeddings learn continuous geometry, and which wins depends heavily on how much data exists per category and how smoothly categories relate to each other. The geometry of a learned embedding space is not automatically interpretable; nearby points suggest similarity but the individual coordinate directions rarely have a clean, nameable meaning on their own, a genuine limitation when someone asks a model to explain why two stations were treated similarly.

At production scale, embedding tables for systems with millions of categories, users, items, locations, become the single largest source of model parameters and memory footprint, which drives specialized infrastructure, parameter servers, embedding sharding across many machines, and quantized or hashed embedding tables, purpose-built to store and update them efficiently, well beyond what a single-machine PyTorch embedding layer handles. Cold-start remains a genuinely unsolved production problem at scale: systems typically fall back to hierarchical embeddings, embed a broader category, like freeway segment, when the specific one, station, has too little data, or hybrid approaches that blend a learned embedding with hand-built features until enough data accumulates. An active research and engineering question is how embeddings learned for one task transfer to related but distinct tasks and domains without full retraining, which matters enormously for cost at scale but remains only partially solved, with transfer sometimes working well and sometimes silently degrading performance in ways that are hard to predict ahead of time.

gaussian-process.def: A model that predicts not just one number but a whole range of likely curves, giving wider uncertainty where it has seen less data.
levels: Imagine drawing a squiggly line through some dots, but around your line you also draw a fuzzy cloud showing how sure you are, a thin cloud where you have lots of dots nearby, and a big fat cloud where you are just guessing. A Gaussian process draws that line and that cloud together.

A Gaussian process is a way for a model to predict not just a single guess, but a range of reasonable guesses, along with how confident it is. Where it has seen a lot of similar examples, its guess is confident and the range is narrow; where it has seen very little data, it admits it is unsure and gives a wide range. This is different from most models, which just give one number and no sense of how trustworthy that number is.

A Gaussian process defines a probability distribution over entire functions, not just over individual values, using a kernel, a similarity function, that says how strongly two points' predictions should influence each other based on how close together they are. Given some observed points, it produces a predicted mean curve plus a confidence band, the variance, around it at every point, and that band widens automatically in regions with no nearby observed data. Fitting one usually means choosing a kernel, like a periodic kernel for a daily traffic pattern, and tuning its hyperparameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the observed data.

Formally, a Gaussian process is a collection of random variables, any finite subset of which has a joint Gaussian, normal, distribution, fully specified by a mean function and a covariance, kernel, function; the kernel encodes prior assumptions about smoothness, periodicity, or other structure the modeler expects the true function to have. Predicting at a new point is a closed-form Bayesian update: conditioning the joint Gaussian on the observed points gives an exact posterior mean and variance at any new input, which is what produces both the predicted curve and its uncertainty band without needing iterative optimization for prediction itself, only for fitting kernel hyperparameters. It fails to scale well: exact inference requires inverting an n by n matrix of pairwise similarities between all observed points, which costs cubic time in the number of points and becomes impractical past a few thousand data points, a serious limitation for anything approaching typical dataset sizes in this course's traffic data. The choice of kernel matters enormously and is itself a modeling decision with real consequences; a smooth kernel assumes a smooth underlying function, and using the wrong kernel family produces systematically overconfident or underconfident uncertainty bands.

The kernel is where all of a Gaussian process's assumptions live, and composing kernels, adding a periodic kernel for daily cycles to a smooth kernel for slower trends, for instance, is a principled and common way to encode structured prior knowledge about a signal like a station's daily traffic profile, though choosing and validating a kernel composition is closer to craft than an automated procedure. Sparse and approximate Gaussian process methods, inducing points, variational approximations, exist specifically to address the cubic-time scaling wall, trading some predictive accuracy for tractability on datasets of realistic size, and are what makes Gaussian processes usable at all beyond toy or small-data problems. A common misconception is treating a Gaussian process's uncertainty band as automatically well-calibrated in any absolute sense; it is well-calibrated only relative to the assumed kernel and prior, so a badly chosen kernel produces a confidence band that looks principled but is quietly wrong. Gaussian processes are prized specifically for problems with limited data where honest uncertainty matters more than raw predictive accuracy, a real and different tradeoff from this course's main models, logistic regression, LightGBM, neural nets, which are chosen instead for scalability to a large dataset.

In production settings, Gaussian processes are mostly reserved for problems where data is genuinely scarce and calibrated uncertainty is worth the computational cost; Bayesian optimization for tuning expensive hyperparameters or physical experiments is the most common production use, precisely because each evaluation is costly and a Gaussian process's uncertainty estimate directly guides which point to try next. Deep kernel learning and neural process methods are active research attempts to combine a Gaussian process's calibrated uncertainty with a neural network's ability to scale to large, high-dimensional data, an open problem because the two approaches' strengths, uncertainty quantification versus raw scale, have historically traded off against each other rather than combining cleanly. For a large sensor network like this course's, a full Gaussian process over every station is impractical, but the underlying idea, a model that tells you not just its prediction but how much to trust it, wider where data is thin, remains a genuinely valuable property that cheaper production models try to approximate without paying the Gaussian process's computational cost.

confusion-matrix.def: A table showing how many predictions were correct or wrong, broken down by predicted class versus actual class.
levels: Imagine a chart with four boxes: times you correctly said yes, times you correctly said no, and the two kinds of times you got it wrong. A confusion matrix is exactly that chart, counting up how the model's guesses compared to what actually happened.

A confusion matrix is a small table that shows how a model's predictions compare to the real answers. For a yes or no prediction, it has four boxes: correct yes predictions, true positives, correct no predictions, true negatives, wrong yes predictions when it was actually no, false positives, and wrong no predictions when it was actually yes, false negatives. Looking at these four numbers together tells you a lot more about a model's mistakes than a single percent-correct score would.

For binary classification, the confusion matrix is a 2 by 2 table: true positives, predicted slow and actually slow, false positives, predicted slow but actually not, false negatives, predicted not slow but actually was, and true negatives, predicted not slow and actually not. In scikit-learn, `confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)` computes it directly from the true labels and the model's predicted labels. From these four counts you compute precision, true positives divided by true positives plus false positives, how often a slow prediction was right, and recall, true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives, how much of the real slow traffic the model actually caught.

The confusion matrix requires a classification threshold to exist at all; it is computed from hard predicted labels, 0 or 1, not raw probabilities, so it summarizes the model's behavior at one specific operating point, and a different threshold produces a different confusion matrix from the exact same underlying probabilities. Every standard classification metric, precision, recall, F1, specificity, false positive rate, is a simple ratio computed from the matrix's four cells, which is why the confusion matrix is often described as the source data behind nearly every other binary classification metric. It becomes especially informative, and especially necessary, under class imbalance: with rare slow episodes, a model that always predicts not slow achieves very high accuracy while its confusion matrix immediately reveals zero true positives and zero recall, exposing a failure that accuracy alone hides. It fails to summarize model quality across the full range of possible thresholds on its own, since it is a snapshot at one threshold; a precision-recall curve or ROC curve instead shows how the matrix's implied metrics change as the threshold varies.

Precision and recall trade off against each other as the threshold moves, and which one to prioritize is a decision about the real-world cost of each error type; for a slow-traffic alert system, missing a real slow episode, a false negative, may be far more costly than a false alarm, a false positive, which argues for choosing a lower threshold and accepting more false positives, a decision the confusion matrix alone cannot make but directly informs. Confusion matrices generalize to multi-class problems as an n by n table, where off-diagonal cells show specifically which classes get confused with which others, more diagnostically useful than a single accuracy number for understanding a multi-class model's specific failure modes. A common misconception is treating precision and recall as properties of the model itself, when they are really properties of the model at a chosen threshold; reporting them without stating the threshold, or comparing two models' precision and recall at different, unstated thresholds, is a subtle but real source of misleading comparisons. Normalized confusion matrices, showing rates rather than raw counts, per true class or per predicted class, are often more useful than raw counts for imbalanced data, since raw counts on the majority class can visually dwarf the minority class's counts even when the minority class's error rate is the one that actually matters.

In production monitoring, confusion matrices, and the metrics derived from them, are tracked continuously per-segment, per station, per time of day, per region, rather than as a single aggregate number, because a model with acceptable overall precision and recall can still perform badly for a specific slice of the population, and aggregate metrics hide that the way accuracy hides class imbalance. Threshold selection in production is typically not fixed once at training time but tuned or re-tuned against the confusion matrix computed on recent live data, since the right operating point can drift as the underlying distribution of traffic patterns shifts over time, seasonal changes, new construction, altered commute patterns. An open practical challenge is building monitoring systems that can detect a meaningful degradation in one cell of the confusion matrix, say, a rising false-negative rate for a specific corridor, quickly enough to act on it, without either drowning in noisy per-slice metrics or missing a real regression by only watching the aggregate numbers.

categorical.def: Categorical data takes on a fixed set of named values, like freeway direction; one-hot and ordinal are two ways to turn it into numbers a model can use.
levels: Some things come as words, not numbers, like red, blue, or green, or north and south for which way a road goes. Categorical just means the answer is a word from a fixed list, not a number you could measure with a ruler.

A categorical feature is one that takes a value from a fixed set of categories, like the direction of a freeway, north, south, east, west, or a station's freeway number, rather than a number you can do arithmetic on directly. Since most models only understand numbers, categorical data has to be converted somehow: one-hot encoding makes a separate 0-or-1 column for each possible category, and ordinal encoding just assigns each category a number, 0, 1, 2, and so on, which only makes sense if the categories actually have a real order.

One-hot encoding turns a column with k categories into k separate columns of 0s and 1s, with exactly one 1 per row marking which category that row belongs to; in pandas, `pd.get_dummies(df["direction"])` does this. Ordinal encoding instead assigns each category an integer, like Monday equals 0 through Sunday equals 6, appropriate only when the categories have a genuine order; using ordinal encoding on something with no real order, like freeway direction, would falsely tell the model that east is somehow between north and south numerically. Some models, notably LightGBM, can take a categorical column natively, marked with a category dtype, without either encoding, and handle the splitting internally in a way that avoids the blown-up column count of one-hot encoding.

One-hot encoding is the safe general-purpose choice for models like linear and logistic regression that assume a linear relationship between a feature's numeric value and the outcome, since it makes no false assumption about ordering, but it has a real cost: a column with many categories, like station_id, with hundreds of unique values, produces hundreds of new sparse columns, which increases dimensionality and can hurt models sensitive to it. Ordinal encoding is more compact but only valid when categories genuinely have an order, day of week has one, freeway direction does not, and misapplying it to an unordered category introduces a false numeric structure that can seriously mislead a linear model, though tree-based models are somewhat more forgiving since they only ever use the ordering to define split thresholds, not to assume linear spacing. Native categorical support in tree-based libraries like LightGBM avoids both problems by finding an optimal grouping of categories directly during tree building, without expanding the column count or imposing a false order, generally the best option for high-cardinality categoricals when using a tree-based model. It fails, for one-hot encoding specifically, when a category seen at prediction time was never seen during training, a brand-new station added later, since there is no corresponding one-hot column for it, which needs to be handled explicitly, an unknown category, or falling back to some default.

High-cardinality categorical features, many unique categories, like station_id with hundreds of values, push practitioners toward target encoding or embeddings instead of one-hot, since both keep dimensionality low while still letting the model learn a numeric representation that reflects how the category actually relates to the target, but target encoding specifically introduces leakage risk if not computed carefully with proper cross-validation folds; encoding a category by its own target's average, without holding out the row itself, silently leaks the label into the feature. The choice between one-hot, ordinal, native categorical, and learned embeddings is not purely a matter of correctness but of what each model architecture can actually exploit: linear models benefit most from one-hot's lack of false structure, tree models benefit most from native categorical or well-chosen ordinal groupings, and neural networks benefit most from learned embeddings that can place similar categories near each other in a continuous space. A frequent practitioner mistake is one-hot encoding a feature with a natural but non-uniform order instead of a more informative ordinal or target encoding, discarding real ordering information the model could have used. Category drift between training and serving, new categories appearing, old ones disappearing, or their relative frequency shifting, needs to be actively monitored rather than assumed away, since most encoding schemes handle unseen categories poorly by default and fail silently rather than raising an obvious error.

At production scale, categorical feature handling is one of the most consequential and error-prone parts of a real feature pipeline, because encoding logic, the mapping from category to number, has to be computed once and then applied identically at both training and serving time; any mismatch, a category encoded differently, or an unseen category handled differently, is a classic and hard-to-debug source of train and serve skew. Large-scale recommendation and search systems, which deal with categorical features numbering in the millions, user IDs, item IDs, rely heavily on learned embeddings with hashing tricks to keep the representation size bounded regardless of how many distinct categories exist, accepting a small, controlled amount of hash collision in exchange for tractable memory use. An open engineering problem at scale is managing categorical feature schemas over time as a living, versioned artifact, tracking which categories existed when a given model was trained, so that a category's meaning and its encoding can be audited and reproduced long after the fact, not just handled correctly in the moment.

duckdb.def: DuckDB is an embedded analytical database that runs SQL queries directly over files like Parquet or CSV, with no server to set up.
levels: Imagine a filing cabinet that can also do math for you, like counting how many red folders you have, just by asking it a question instead of counting yourself. DuckDB is like that: a database you can ask questions of, that lives right inside your project instead of needing its own separate computer.

DuckDB is a database, a tool for storing and asking questions about large tables of data, that runs entirely inside your own program without needing a separate server to set up or connect to. You can point it directly at a file, like a Parquet or CSV file of traffic readings, and ask it questions using SQL, a language designed for questions like how many rows have speed below 30. SQLite is a similar idea, a database that lives in a single file with no server, but DuckDB is built specifically to be fast at exactly this kind of ask-a-question-across-millions-of-rows analytical query.

A basic DuckDB query looks like `SELECT station_id, AVG(speed) FROM 'readings.parquet' GROUP BY station_id`, which DuckDB can run directly against a Parquet file on disk without first loading it all into a table. Its core SQL vocabulary includes `SELECT`, choose columns, `WHERE`, filter rows, `GROUP BY`, aggregate per group, like pandas's groupby, `JOIN`, combine two tables on a shared key, and window functions, compute something like a running total across ordered rows without collapsing them into groups. Unlike SQLite, which is designed for many small, quick read and write transactions, DuckDB is designed for scanning and aggregating large amounts of data quickly, exactly the kind of work a how-many-slow-episodes-happened-last-month question needs.

DuckDB is a columnar, vectorized query engine, meaning it stores and processes data column-by-column rather than row-by-row and operates on batches of values at once, which is why it can scan and aggregate a large Parquet file dramatically faster than an equivalent row-by-row Python loop, or often even faster than pandas for large aggregations, despite running on a single machine with no separate server process. It can query Parquet files directly without a separate load step, using Parquet's own columnar structure and metadata, min and max statistics per column chunk, to skip reading data it does not need for a given filter, a major reason it beats reading the whole file into memory first. It fails to help, or is simply unnecessary overhead, for small datasets that already comfortably fit in memory and are only touched with pandas-native operations, where DuckDB's setup and the mental overhead of writing SQL do not pay for themselves. SQLite, by contrast, excels at many small, frequent read and write operations from an application, a different workload, transactional, not analytical, from the run-one-big-aggregation-over-months-of-sensor-readings pattern this course's traffic data needs.

The distinction between DuckDB and SQLite reflects the standard OLAP versus OLTP split in database design: OLTP is optimized for many small transactions that read and write individual rows reliably and often concurrently, while OLAP is optimized for scanning and aggregating huge amounts of data for analysis, and using the wrong one for a workload works but performs poorly compared to the tool built for that job. DuckDB's ability to query Parquet, CSV, and even pandas DataFrames directly, without an explicit import or load step, blurs the traditional line between a file on disk and a database table in a way that is genuinely useful for exploratory analysis, letting a practitioner move fluidly between SQL and pandas on the same underlying data without duplicating it. A common practitioner mistake is reaching for pandas by default for every aggregation, even ones that are naturally expressed and executed far faster as a single SQL query over a Parquet file, simply out of familiarity with the pandas API. DuckDB's SQL implementation includes fairly complete window function support, running totals, ranks, lag and lead within a partition, which mirrors much of what groupby plus shift or rolling does in pandas, and for large datasets, expressing that logic in SQL executed by DuckDB can be substantially faster than the equivalent pandas code.

At production data-pipeline scale, DuckDB is increasingly used as a fast, embedded analytical layer inside larger systems, for local development against a sample of production-scale data, for lightweight ETL steps, or embedded directly into an application needing fast local analytics without standing up and operating a full database server, precisely because it needs no separate infrastructure to deploy or maintain. It sits in an interesting middle position in the broader analytical-engine landscape: faster and lower-overhead than distributed systems like Spark for data that fits on one machine, but without Spark's ability to scale out across a cluster once data genuinely exceeds single-machine memory and disk, the open tradeoff practitioners weigh when a dataset's growth trajectory is uncertain. An active area of development in the broader ecosystem is improving interoperability between DuckDB, pandas, Polars, and Arrow-based tools so that data can move between them with minimal copying, since today crossing between these tools still sometimes involves real serialization cost that undercuts the speed advantage any single one of them offers.

conda.def: Package and environment managers for Python; conda installs both Python packages and non-Python system libraries, and miniforge is a minimal, open-source way to get conda.
levels: Imagine a special toolbox that not only holds your tools but also comes with its own tiny hardware store attached, in case a tool needs a part that is not in the box yet. conda is like that for Python: it manages both your project's toolbox and the extra bits those tools sometimes need underneath.

conda is a tool, like pip, for installing the packages, bundles of code, a Python project needs, but it can also install things that are not Python at all, like the underlying math libraries some packages depend on. miniforge is a small, free way to get conda installed on your computer without extra, unnecessary software bundled in. Both let you create separate environments, one per project, so installing something for one project cannot accidentally break another.

conda manages environments with commands like `conda create -n myenv python=3.11`, make a new environment, and `conda activate myenv`, switch into it, and installs packages with `conda install numpy`. Unlike pip, which only installs Python packages and assumes any non-Python dependencies, like a specific BLAS math library, are already present on your system, conda can install and manage those underlying non-Python dependencies itself, which matters for scientific packages like numpy and LightGBM that rely on fast, compiled math code underneath. miniforge is a minimal installer for conda that defaults to the free, community-run conda-forge package channel rather than Anaconda's own channel, which has licensing restrictions for some commercial use.

conda's core advantage over pip is that it resolves a dependency graph across both Python and non-Python packages together; it understands that a specific version of numpy needs a specific version of a BLAS library, and picks compatible versions of everything at once, whereas pip mostly just installs the specific Python packages you list, assuming their non-Python system dependencies already exist correctly on the machine. This makes conda especially valuable on Apple silicon, where the difference between an arm64-native BLAS backend and one running under Rosetta emulation directly affects both correctness in edge cases and, more commonly, performance, sometimes dramatically so. It fails to be simple in one specific, well-known way: conda's own dependency solver can be very slow, especially on complex environments with many packages, to the point that solving an environment can take minutes; mamba, a drop-in faster reimplementation of the same solver, exists specifically to fix this, and miniforge ships with it by default. Mixing pip and conda installs in the same environment works in the common case but can produce subtly broken environments if pip overwrites a package conda installed with a version conda does not know about, so most guidance is to install everything possible with conda first and use pip only for what is unavailable there.

The core distinction that matters for reproducibility is that a `requirements.txt` file, pip, generally only pins Python package versions and implicitly assumes a compatible system environment already exists, while a conda environment file can pin the full dependency graph, including compiled system libraries, closer to what is genuinely needed to reproduce identical numerical results across machines, though even conda does not fully solve this, since the compiler and hardware that built a given binary package can still introduce tiny numerical differences. Lock files, conda-lock, or pip-tools and uv for the pip side, exist to freeze not just the top-level packages requested but the entire resolved dependency tree to exact versions and hashes, which is what actually makes an environment reproducible a year later, since an unpinned environment file can resolve to different package versions today than it did when the project was created. A common practitioner mistake is treating an environment file without exact version pins as reproducible, when in fact re-running `conda create` from it later can silently pull newer package versions that behave differently, sometimes producing different numeric results from the same code. conda-forge's community-maintained package builds, which miniforge defaults to, have become the de facto standard for reproducible scientific Python environments specifically because of broad, consistent arm64 support that matters a great deal for Apple silicon users doing exactly this kind of ML work.

At production and research infrastructure scale, conda and pip-based environment management is often superseded by containerization or fully hermetic build systems precisely because neither conda nor pip fully captures every factor that can change numerical results, OS-level libraries, compiler flags, hardware-specific optimizations, which matters enormously when a research claim or a production model's behavior needs to be reproducible across different machines and over time. Even so, conda environments, or their pip equivalents, usually live inside those containers as the layer that actually manages Python-level dependencies, so the tools are complementary rather than competing once a project matures past a single researcher's laptop. An open, still-real practical problem across the industry is that despite lock files, containers, and careful pinning, floating-point non-determinism from different hardware, driver versions, and even multi-threaded execution order continues to make bit-for-bit reproducibility of ML training genuinely hard to achieve, which is why most reproducibility claims in practice settle for reproducible within acceptable tolerance rather than exact.

observed.def: PeMS's `% Observed` column: the share of a station's 5-minute reading that came from real sensor samples rather than being imputed from neighbors or history.
levels: Sometimes a sensor on the road is having a bad day and cannot see everything, so the traffic computer has to guess the missing bits using nearby sensors, like filling in a puzzle piece with a similar-looking one. Percent Observed is a number that tells you how much of a reading was the sensor's real answer versus a guess.

Percent Observed, also written pct_obs, is a column PeMS provides that tells you what fraction of a station's five-minute reading actually came from real sensor measurements, versus being filled in, or imputed, from nearby stations and past history when the sensor was not fully working. A value of 100 percent means every sample behind that reading was real; a lower value means some or all of it was estimated rather than measured. This matters because a reading built mostly from imputation is less trustworthy than one built entirely from real measurements, even though both look like an ordinary number in the data.

PeMS aggregates each detector's raw samples, often 30-second readings, up to 5-minute rows, and Percent Observed reports what percentage of the samples behind that 5-minute row were real sensor readings rather than values PeMS itself imputed from nearby stations or recent history when the sensor was down or malfunctioning. Aggregate columns, like flow, are computed as a flow-weighted average across all lanes at that station, and Percent Observed reflects the reliability of that whole aggregation, not just one lane. A station with a consistently low Percent Observed over time is a sign of a partially or fully broken sensor, worth flagging or excluding rather than trusting at face value.

Percent Observed functions as a data-quality signal that is separate from, but correlated with, whether a value is present at all in the grid; a station can have a full row of numbers, no missing NaN, that is still mostly imputed, a distinct and easy-to-miss failure mode from an outright missing reading, since a naive missingness check on the value alone would not catch it. Using it well typically means building a detector-health score that combines Percent Observed, internal consistency between flow and occupancy, checked against the station's own historical flow-occupancy relationship, sometimes called its fundamental diagram, and agreement with neighboring stations' readings, rather than trusting any single signal alone. It fails to fully solve the missing-data problem on its own: a station could have high Percent Observed but the underlying sensor could still be systematically miscalibrated, reporting real but wrong values, which Percent Observed alone would not reveal, since it only measures how much of the reading was directly sampled versus imputed, not whether the sampled values themselves are accurate.

Percent Observed is a useful but imperfect proxy for trustworthiness because PeMS's own imputation, when Percent Observed is low, already leans on neighboring stations and recent history, which means a low-Percent-Observed reading is not simply missing data but a smoothed, possibly overly-conservative estimate that can itself distort downstream features like lag or rolling averages if used without adjustment or a lower weight. A subtlety practitioners often miss is that Percent Observed is reported per aggregated row, but the underlying imputation happens at the sample or lane level before aggregation, so two rows with the same Percent Observed number can have arrived at that number through very different patterns of which lanes or samples were actually missing. Building features or filtering rules purely from a Percent Observed threshold, say, dropping anything below 90 percent, is a reasonable first pass but risks discarding a meaningful share of real data during periods of partial sensor trouble that are not evenly distributed across time or stations, which can itself introduce a systematic bias, certain times of day or certain stations disproportionately excluded. Comparing Percent Observed against independent cross-checks, like agreement with immediate neighbors or the station's own historical flow-occupancy relationship, is a more robust way to build genuine confidence in a reading than trusting Percent Observed in isolation.

In production sensor-network systems generally, a per-reading data-quality or confidence signal like Percent Observed is standard practice, and mature pipelines treat it as a first-class feature, feeding it into the model itself, weighting training examples by it, or using it to gate which readings even enter the training set, rather than discarding it after an initial filtering pass. Detector health monitoring at scale, flagging which of potentially thousands of sensors are degrading, not just which single readings are currently unreliable, is a genuinely separate and important system from any individual model's data-quality handling, since a sensor beginning to fail is itself an actionable signal, dispatch a technician, independent of any downstream prediction task. An open practical question in sensor-heavy ML systems broadly is how to properly propagate reading-level uncertainty, of which Percent Observed is one example, all the way through feature engineering into a model's own predictive uncertainty, rather than treating data quality and model uncertainty as two disconnected concerns handled by entirely separate parts of the pipeline.

model-eval.def: `model.eval()` puts a PyTorch model into evaluation mode, turning off training-only behavior like dropout and freezing batch norm statistics.
levels: Imagine a student who studies with extra distractions on purpose to get better at focusing, but then removes those distractions during the actual test. `model.eval()` tells the model this is the real test now, so it stops doing the extra tricks it only needed while practicing.

`model.eval()` is a command in PyTorch that switches a neural network from training mode into evaluation, or testing, mode. Some layers, like dropout, behave differently during training than during actual use: dropout randomly turns off some connections while training, to prevent overfitting, but should not do that when you are actually asking the model for a real prediction. Calling `model.eval()` before making predictions turns off those training-only behaviors so the model gives its best, most stable answer.

`model.eval()` changes the behavior of specific layer types: dropout layers stop randomly zeroing out values and instead pass everything through unchanged, and batch normalization layers stop computing statistics from the current batch and instead use the fixed running average statistics they accumulated during training. The opposite call, `model.train()`, switches back to training-mode behavior for these same layers. Forgetting to call `model.eval()` before evaluating or deploying a model is a common bug: the model will still run and produce output, but that output will be noisier and less consistent than it should be, because dropout is still randomly active.

`model.eval()` and `model.train()` are mode switches, not separate models; they toggle a training flag that layers like dropout and batch normalization check internally to decide which code path to run, which is why the model's architecture and learned weights are unchanged either way, only the behavior of a specific handful of layer types changes. Batch normalization is the subtler of the two: during training, it normalizes each batch using that batch's own mean and variance while also updating a running estimate of the population mean and variance; in eval mode, it switches to using that accumulated running estimate instead, since a single prediction, or a batch of size 1, has no meaningful batch statistics of its own to normalize with. It fails silently, not with an error, when forgotten: a model left in training mode during evaluation will still produce output, and that output can look plausible, exactly what makes this a dangerous bug, reported evaluation metrics can be worse, from dropout's added noise, or, particularly with a badly calibrated batch norm running estimate, meaningfully different from the model's true deployed behavior.

The eval and train distinction is entangled with a second, separate PyTorch concept, gradient tracking, and conflating them is a common practitioner mistake: `model.eval()` changes layer behavior but does not, by itself, stop PyTorch from building the computational graph needed for backpropagation, so `torch.no_grad()`, or `torch.inference_mode()`, its newer, stricter variant, is also needed during evaluation to actually save memory and computation by skipping gradient tracking; using eval mode without no_grad is correct but wasteful, and using no_grad without eval mode leaves dropout and batch norm running in training mode, producing wrong results. Batch normalization's running statistics, accumulated via an exponential moving average with a momentum hyperparameter during training, can be poorly calibrated if training used very small batch sizes or ended early, a real and somewhat hidden cause of a model performing noticeably worse in eval mode than its training-mode metrics suggested. Newer normalization schemes, like layer normalization, standard in transformers, do not have this train and eval distinction at all, since they normalize across features within a single example rather than across a batch, which sidesteps this entire class of bug at the cost of a different set of tradeoffs.

In production inference systems, correctly setting eval mode, and disabling gradient tracking, is a basic but consequential deployment step that gets automated away in serving frameworks specifically because forgetting it in hand-written serving code is a well-known, recurring class of bug that silently degrades a deployed model's quality without raising any error. Model export and conversion pipelines for on-device deployment, like converting a PyTorch model to Core ML for an Apple device, need to correctly fold batch normalization's running statistics into the exported model's fixed weights, since the target runtime typically does not implement PyTorch's train and eval distinction at all, it only ever runs in the equivalent of eval mode. An open practical concern at scale is train and serve skew introduced by exactly this kind of mode mismatch, subtle enough to pass basic testing but capable of degrading real-world model quality, which is why serving infrastructure increasingly includes automated checks that compare a served model's output against its original training-time evaluation output on a fixed test set, specifically to catch this class of bug before it reaches production traffic.

sorted.def: A family of Python built-ins for working with sequences: `sorted` orders items, `len` counts them, `sum` adds them, and `map`/`filter` transform or select items.
levels: Imagine a magic box of tools: one tool lines up your toys from smallest to biggest, one counts how many toys you have, one adds up how much they all weigh together, and two more tools help you change or pick out just the toys you want. These are five of Python's basic built-in tools for working with a list of things.

`sorted(list)` returns a new list with the items arranged in order, smallest to largest by default, without changing the original list. `len(list)` tells you how many items are in it, and `sum(list)` adds up all the numbers in it. `map(function, list)` applies a function to every item and gives you back the results, and `filter(function, list)` keeps only the items where the function returns true, throwing the rest away.

`sorted(counts, reverse=True)` sorts a list from largest to smallest instead of the default smallest to largest; sorted can also take a key argument, like `sorted(stations, key=lambda s: s.postmile)`, to sort by something other than the plain value. `len(df)` gives the number of rows in a table, and `sum(df["flow"])` adds a column's values, though pandas's own `.sum()` method is generally faster for a whole column. `list(map(str, numbers))` converts every number in a list to text, and `list(filter(lambda x: x > 0, numbers))` keeps only the positive ones; both map and filter return a lazy iterator in Python 3, so wrapping them in `list()` is what actually produces a usable list of results.

These are Python's core built-in functions for the operate-on-every-item-in-a-sequence pattern, and understanding when to use them versus a list comprehension is mostly a matter of readability: `[str(x) for x in numbers]` does the same thing as `list(map(str, numbers))` and is generally considered more idiomatic modern Python, while map and filter remain common, especially when the transformation is already a named function rather than a short inline expression. sorted's default comparison uses each item's natural ordering, numeric comparison for numbers, alphabetical for strings, and Python's sort, Timsort, is stable, meaning items that compare equal keep their original relative order, which matters when sorting by one key but wanting ties broken by original position. len and sum are simple but not free: len is constant time for a list, Python tracks the length directly, but calling sum on a large pure-Python list is linear time and, for numeric data, considerably slower than the equivalent vectorized numpy or pandas operation. It fails, or rather is the wrong tool, once you are working inside a pandas DataFrame or numpy array rather than a plain Python list, since pandas's own `.sum()`, `.sort_values()`, and vectorized filtering are implemented in fast compiled code and are typically far faster than looping with these Python built-ins over DataFrame rows.

The Python-versus-vectorized-library performance gap for these operations is not a minor detail in ML code; `sum()` or a Python-level loop over a numpy array or pandas Series can be one to two orders of magnitude slower than `.sum()` called directly on the array or Series, because the built-in must repeatedly call back into slow, interpreted Python for each element, while the library method runs a tight loop entirely in compiled code. sorted with a key function has a real cost consideration too: the key function is called exactly once per item, Python caches the computed keys internally, so an expensive key function is not a performance trap the way a naive re-computation on every comparison would be. filter and map, being lazy iterators, are memory-efficient for large sequences since they do not materialize the full result until consumed, but this laziness is also a common source of bugs: a filter or map object can only be iterated once, so code that tries to loop over the same filter result twice silently gets nothing the second time, which surprises practitioners coming from languages where such operations return a reusable list. A frequent practitioner mistake in ML code specifically is writing a Python-level loop with these built-ins over rows of a DataFrame or elements of a numpy array purely out of familiarity, when the equivalent vectorized call is both shorter and dramatically faster.

At production scale, none of these built-ins is typically the bottleneck in a mature ML pipeline, precisely because performance-sensitive code paths have already moved to vectorized numpy and pandas operations, compiled kernels, or a database engine; where these Python built-ins remain common is in glue code, configuration processing, and small-scale bookkeeping around the edges of a pipeline, where readability matters more than raw speed. Their real ongoing relevance in a large, mature codebase is less about performance and more about code review and correctness discipline: a reviewer needs to recognize when a straightforward for loop with sum or sorted over what looks like a small list is secretly being called on a large or growing collection in production, silently becoming a performance problem as data volume scales up over time. This is a small but real instance of a broader production lesson: code that is correct and fine in a notebook or a small test can become a real bottleneck once it runs at the actual scale and frequency of a production system, and the fix is almost always switching from a Python-level loop or built-in to the equivalent vectorized or database-native operation, not micro-optimizing the Python loop itself.
